entries.title: Senate Overwhelmingly Approves Bill to Avoid October Shutdown
entries.summary: The measure includes a provision that blocks the Trump administration from controlling state grants, but the bill’s fate is unclear in the House.
entries.content:
The Senate overwhelmingly passed a bipartisan measure funding federal agencies until mid-December early on Saturday morning, putting Congress on track to avert a government shutdown in October and kicking funding negotiations until after the midterm elections.

Senators voted 90-6 to approve a bill that extends current funding levels through Dec. 11, with some exceptions. Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, told reporters that the measure is a positive step after a number of government shutdowns over the past year.

“I believe that we all want to make sure that we have good funding through Dec. 11 and hopefully we’ll be able to negotiate good bills once the elections are over,” Murray said.

The Senate’s stopgap funding bill, though, is different from the version the House passed in July. The Senate measure includes a provision Democrats demanded that would delay a Trump administration rule putting political appointees in charge of issuing grants.

It’s unclear whether House Republicans will take up the Senate’s bill when the chamber returns in September –– the House and Senate must approve identical funding packages in order to avoid a government shutdown.

“Many of us felt very strongly about it, so it's in there,” Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who chairs the Appropriations panel, told reporters of the grant provision. “Our focus is on getting the continuing resolution through and preventing a government shutdown.”

The vote on the continuing resolution was delayed for several days, in part over a provision that pushes back the date a ban on intoxicating hemp is implemented. Senators voted an amendment that failed to implement those restrictions come October alongside the funding bill.

The Senate also punted a vote a party-line budget bill that would have kick-started the process to fund some of Republicans’ most pressing priorities, including the war in Iran and new voter ID requirements demanded by President Donald Trump.

Senators on both sides of the aisle seem to be gearing up for a bigger fight over funding in December. Any government spending bill needs 60 votes to pass in the upper chamber, giving Democrats some leverage.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana), another appropriator, told reporters that he and other Republicans are prepared to fight to reinstate the Trump administration’s language on grants after the midterms.

Kennedy added that it’s his understanding that federal agencies would not have been able to implement the rule by December, regardless of the delay included in the Senate’s funding bill.

“This CR only extends until December 11, but I’m not going to be surprised if we don’t have another CR after,” Kennedy said. “And I’m going to fight like hell to make sure there is no impediment to the rule, because it’s a good rule.”

Senate Democrats agreed they expect the provision to become a sticking point in December. Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, another appropriator, told NOTUS that he wants to see Democrats push back on any effort to revive the administration’s grant rule.

“One of the things that I thought was really important was Sen. Collins and Sen. Murray were able to come to an agreement to defer a really destructive [Office of Management and Budget] rule,” Coons said. “That rule should never be allowed to come into force.”

Murray said Democrats are focused on pushing their funding priorities forward in December, adding that she thinks the biggest outstanding question is how much to spend on defense, given the continued U.S. war against Iran.

“We need to find a defense, non-defense top line that is rational and that we can work with,” Murray said.

Defense spending has already become an issue for some Democrats. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine opposed the funding bill, saying he will not vote for government funding until the war in Iran is finished.

Kaine said he isn’t expecting other Democrats to join him in voting down government funding over the war, but added that the power of the purse is an important negotiation point for Democrats.

“It's the only tool we have,” Kaine told NOTUS. “I think the work product is great. It's just that I don't feel comfortable giving a green light to a whole lot of government funding in the middle of an illegal war.”

West Virginia Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, a top Republican leader, said the next round of negotiations on government funding will probably come down to one thing.

“There’s always sticking points,” Capito said. “A lot of it is going to depend on who wins the election.”

entries.title: Senate Confirms Todd Blanche as Attorney General
entries.summary: His promotion overcame significant questions from Republicans about his handling of Trump’s controversial settlement with the IRS.
entries.content:
The Senate voted mostly along party lines 50-49 to confirm Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, capping off weeks of intense talks regarding his leadership capacity and delay in promising to kill President Donald Trump’s controversial IRS settlement deal provisions.

Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins joined Democrats early Saturday morning to vote against his confirmation. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) was still absent following his release from a rehabilitation facility earlier in the week.

Blanche took over as acting attorney general after the president ousted Pam Bondi in April. But his full promotion to the country’s top law enforcement post was dubious after Republican holdouts took issue with the IRS’s settlement with Trump that gave him and certain family members immunity from tax audits and created a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund that could pay out those who felt they had been wronged by the federal government, including Jan. 6 riot participants.

Blanche’s critics grilled him over the course of his confirmation process for his handling of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and whether he’d remain an enforcer of Trump’s agenda, which has included attempted indictments of the president's opponents. During a closed-door House Oversight interview in May, Bondi blamed Blanche for mismanaging the investigation into Epstein.

Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) initially took issue with the IRS settlement provisions, threatening to block Blanche from advancing out of the Senate Judiciary Committee unless he delivered written assurances to quell their concerns.

Their impasse broke once Blanche complied with Cornyn and Tillis’ demands to nix the fund and limit the immunity’s deal scope, though the document’s enforceability is still in question, as is whether he will uphold it now that he has been confirmed.

Trump, who once employed Blanche as his personal lawyer, repeatedly suggested throughout the senators’ blockade that he would pull the nomination and leave Blanche as acting attorney general if he did not have enough votes, or wait until Tillis and Cornyn exited Congress next year.

Collins and Murkowski said they would vote against him in statements. The deciding factor came down to outgoing Sen. Bill Cassidy (R–Louisiana), who defended Blanche in a floor speech hours before the chamber was set to vote.

“Mr. Blanche is not perfect, and he will tell you this.” Cassidy said Friday. “But the choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche. It is between Mr. Blanche and another acting attorney general who may not run the department effectively under President Trump.”

In addition to ongoing litigation involving the Epstein files and the IRS settlement, the Justice Department is still contending with midterm election security and recent changes within its civil rights division, among other issues.

entries.title: Iran Releases Set of Demands to Reopen the Strait of Hormuz
entries.summary: The wide-ranging demands jeopardize a deal to reopen a waterway crucial to the global energy market.
entries.content:
A senior Iranian government official declared Saturday that the Strait of Hormuz would not open until the Trump administration meets a wide-ranging set of demands.

Iranian security official Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr wrote in a statement that the United States must lift its naval blockade of the crucial waterway on the Persian Gulf, end sanctions against the country, release frozen Iranian assets, end the war in Iran and pay restitution for its damages.

The statement, which was circulated by Iranian state media, said the strait would not open “until America corrects its behavior.”

Iran’s demands jeopardize a deal to reopen the strait that several White House officials were optimistic would be reached earlier this week.

The United States resumed a naval blockade of the strait on July 14, escalating retaliatory attacks on Iran as a memorandum of understanding between the two countries seemingly collapsed. Negotiations bittered — as the U.S. military’s stockpile of missiles has reportedly dwindled — in the weeks since.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC Aug. 4 the agreement would provide “freedom of movement” for commercial ships when asked whether Iran would be allowed to charge a toll.

Bessent predicted oil prices will drop once vessels return to their shipping routes, bringing “relief” to the economy as prices go down, adding: “It’s not just energy. It’s fertilizer, it’s refined products, it is the various industrial gasses.”

The Iranian government has said it is in discussions only with Oman, not the U.S., which drew President Donald Trump’s ire earlier this month. He called Iranian leadership “duplicitous.”

“Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished,” Trump wrote on Truth Social this week. “Whether Iran wants to admit it or not, we are, in fact, talking of a solution to a problem that they have caused, for decades.”

The president called off threats to heavily bomb Iran in early August so negotiations could continue.

entries.title: Senate Doesn’t Vote on College Sports Bill Before Recess
entries.content:
At the first hearing for the Protect College Sports Act in June, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) acknowledged the strange nature of his alliance with Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington), his co-sponsor on the bill. He and Cantwell, Cruz said, probably couldn’t have agreed on the color of the sky before walking into the Hart Building that morning, let alone most issues of substance. But college sports, Cruz explained, is a unifier, a way for Democrats and Republicans to come together, hold hands, agree just enough for the sake of the great American traditions of mascot pushups and watching Penn State blow the big game.

College sports, however, are never just about college sports.

For more than five years now, ever since lobbying picked up in the name, image and likeness (NIL) era, that’s been especially true in Congress, most recently with the Senate not holding a full vote on the Protect College Sports Act (PCSA) before the August recess. While the Senate expects to pick up the bill in September, not voting this week only tightened the window to pass the bipartisan legislation before the midterms this fall. And in the past few days alone, there were multiple examples of why legislating college sports is complicated, to say the least, and ripe for odd factions forming.

On Wednesday, the AFL-CIO and its sports council, which includes most professional players unions, opposed the bill. On Thursday, the Congressional Black Caucus swung hard against the legislation, too, saying it cannot support it as written. Big Labor and the CBC are regular opponents of any bill that could even be perceived as NCAA-friendly. Later Thursday, three Republican senators — Josh Hawley of Missouri, Tommy Tuberville of Alabama and Jim Banks of Indiana — introduced an amendment to protect existing state laws that ban transgender female athletes from participating in women’s sports. In a letter to senators, the attorneys general from six states raised the same concern.

Tuberville, a former college football coach, has spent his summer rallying fellow Republicans against the PCSA for a variety of reasons. On the other side of the aisle, Sens. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) and Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) have done the same, albeit more privately, according to multiple people familiar with how they’ve approached the bill.

“Some strange, strange bedfellows with this bill, though obviously their reasons for trying to slow it down or crush it altogether are all over the map,” a Republican Senate aide told NOTUS on Friday. “That was always the risk of trying for something that’s really, really sweeping.”

The updated bill text is 171 pages. A major part of it — and a sticking point for many Democrats and outside labor groups — would grant the NCAA conditional antitrust protection to set rules for athlete compensation, eligibility and the transfer portal. Broadly, a lot of Democrats are rejecting the bill as bending to the NCAA and its conferences without the direct involvement of athletes. The AFL-CIO’s statement also stunted additional Democratic support this week, according to a handful of Senate aides.

Republicans, on the other hand, have been more likely to hold off support until the bill meets their wishes on specific issues. They were still filing new amendments into Friday evening, right up until the PCSA was bumped behind more pressing matters. Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida) introduced an amendment to the section that limits further expansion and realignment at the power-conference level, which read as giving Miami and/or Florida State the option to switch leagues in the near future without the penalties the PCSA would impose. The conversation on transgender athletes is not going away, either.

Beyond at least five more weeks of this type of scrutiny for the bill, not voting in August means any eventual action in the House would be on a compressed timeline. In July, it was Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri), one of its original co-sponsors, who said that waiting until after recess in the Senate could really complicate the PCSA’s chances, seeing that his colleagues’ attention would then be split by campaigning and budget negotiations.

“It’s clear that this bill is the only way to save college sports and women’s sports,” Cruz and Schmitt said in a joint statement after midnight Friday. “With the strong support of President Trump, we look forward to him signing the bill on [ESPN] College GameDay in the fall.”

In a separate statement, Cantwell said: “Time may have run out to protect college sports in August but there is plenty of time in September. I’m glad Sen. Thune set a date certain in September to bring it up because the challenges facing student athletes and universities aren’t going away."

Cruz and Schmitt also said Thune has “locked in” a vote for September. Given the proposed amendments, though, and the dissenting opinions on both sides, there should be more negotiating post-recess.

A big reason for the pushback this week was that the bill had real momentum. On July 31, late-night negotiations led to the SEC and Big Ten throwing their support behind the bill, a huge development given the conferences’ collective political influence. In turn, Republican Sen. Todd Young of Indiana, home of the defending national champions in football, a Big Ten team, flipped from against to in favor of the PCSA. Publicly, Cruz and Schmitt expressed confidence it would pass — and by a significant margin — before the August recess. The bill even picked up another pair of bipartisan co-sponsors on Thursday in Sens. John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado) and Pete Ricketts (R-Nebraska).

Four Republicans and four Democrats now have their name on the bill —a type of bipartisanship that has long provided a realistic path to the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster. But all along, a goal of the lead senators had been to land somewhere between 70 and 80 votes in the Senate, according to multiple aides who have worked on the bill. They believe that would give the PCSA the momentum needed to advance through the House before the midterms.

Yet advancing in the House, should the bill get there, is no guarantee either. The compressed timeline is only one factor. Another is the ongoing tensions between the House and Senate. And another is that a number of House Republicans want any broad college sports bill to bar athletes from becoming employees. (The SCORE Act, pushed by House Republicans in 2025, did that. The PCSA states it is neutral on employment.) And then another is the Congressional Black Caucus, which had a major hand in sinking SCORE before it reached a House floor vote.

But there are, of course, some very powerful people behind the PCSA. One of them lives in the White House. After Hawley, Tuberville and Banks introduced their amendment Thursday, the White House clarified, through a public statement, that the bill’s preemption of state laws would not affect existing restrictions for transgender female athletes in women’s sports. And just before 5 p.m. Friday, President Donald Trump posted to Truth Social about the PCSA, urging senators to remain in session until they pass it.

That didn’t happen in the end. We’ll now see what the political pressure is like in September.
entries.author: Jesse Dougherty

entries.title: Joe Biden’s Cancer Has Spread Further Into His Body, His Son Says
entries.summary: The former president is enduring “debilitating” pain, Hunter Biden told the BBC in an interview.
entries.content:
Former President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has metastasized into his bones and spread further into his body, his son Hunter Biden said in a late Friday interview with the BBC.

Hunter Biden said the disease has taken a “very painful” toll on his father, who has remained outspoken on politics since leaving office in 2024.

“It’s very debilitating in many respects,” he continued. “But he’s still out there. He’s still doing his thing. He so believes in this country.”

Biden’s office announced the diagnosis in May 2025, saying he was facing an “aggressive” cancer that was found during a routine medical exam.

The former president completed a course of radiation treatment last October, his office later shared. He also underwent a separate procedure to remove skin cancer cells from his forehead. The office and family have shared few details since.

He is expected to live with cancer for the rest of his life, his wife, Jill Biden, told NBC’s “Today Show” in June.

At 82 years old, Biden was the oldest president in American history by the time he left office. His aides have received intense criticism for allegedly not being forthcoming about the former president’s health — a factor that played into his decision to withdraw from the 2024 presidential election. He has an upcoming memoir scheduled for publication on Nov. 17.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
